api_contract.cpp_signature: class Format { public: static std::string percentage(float value, int precision = 1); };
api_contract.rust_signature: pub struct Format; impl Format { /* associated fns only */ }
api_contract.behavior: Stateless. Confirmed by nm: the ONLY library symbol that survived inlining is `indicators::Format::percentage(float, int)` at 0x402f00 (weak/COMDAT, i.e. a header-inline static member). No instance state, no constructor. In Rust make it a unit struct with associated functions, or a free-function module; do not give it fields.

api_contract.cpp_signature: static std::string percentage(float value, int precision = 1)
api_contract.rust_signature: pub fn percentage_with_precision(value: f32, precision: usize) -> String
api_contract.behavior: Returns format!("{:.*}%", precision, (value * 100.0f32) as f64). Disassembly of 0x402f00: `movd %xmm0,%r15d` (arg is a 4-byte float in xmm0), `movslq %esi,%r14` (arg2 is a 32-bit signed int, sign-extended into ios_base::_M_precision at +0x8), `mulss 0x404040` where 0x404040 = 00 00 c8 42 = 100.0f (FLOAT multiply, result rounded to f32), `cvtss2sd` (promote to double), `_M_insert<double>`, then `__ostream_insert(os, 0x404004, 1)` where 0x404004 = "%" (1 char). Stream flags: `and $0xfffffefb; or $0x4` clears floatfield (fixed|scientific = 0x104) and sets _S_fixed (0x4) == `std::fixed`. Built on a std::ostringstream, returns oss.str(). No rounding/clamping of value, no special-casing of inf/nan.

api_contract.cpp_signature: Format::percentage(v)  // default argument precision = 1 substituted at the call site
api_contract.rust_signature: pub fn percentage(value: f32) -> String  // = percentage_with_precision(value, 1)
api_contract.behavior: Rust has no default arguments, so the C++ default must be split into a second entry point. This mirrors the ABI exactly: there is NO default-argument thunk symbol in the binary; the constant 1 is materialized by the caller (`mov $0x1,%esi; movss 0.33f,%xmm0; call 402f00` for line 4, and `mov $0x2,%esi; movss 0.66f,%xmm0` for line 5). Default precision = 1 is independently confirmed by the inlined `movq $0x1,0x8(%rdx)` in build() and get_percentage().

api_contract.cpp_signature: class ProgressBuilder { int progress_ = 0; int total_ = 100; };
api_contract.rust_signature: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)] pub struct ProgressBuilder { progress: i32, total: i32 }
api_contract.behavior: Default-constructed with `indicators::ProgressBuilder builder;`. Two i32 fields. NOTE: the default values are NOT directly observable — both are overwritten by the chained setters and GCC constant-folded the whole object away (no builder ever materializes on main's stack). {0, 100} is inferred by symmetry with ProgressTracker, whose {0, 100} defaults ARE visible in .rodata. The defaults cannot affect the 5 output lines. Provide `new()` plus `impl Default`.

api_contract.rust_signature: pub fn set_progress(&mut self, v: i32) -> &mut Self
api_contract.behavior: Stores v into progress and returns *this so calls chain. Chaining is proven by the call site `builder.set_progress(60).set_total(200);`. Returning `&mut Self` is the correct Rust translation of the C++ lvalue-reference return; it permits the exact same chained-statement shape in test5.rs. (A by-value `mut self -> Self` builder would also compile but changes the call-site form, so prefer &mut Self.)

api_contract.rust_signature: pub fn set_total(&mut self, v: i32) -> &mut Self
api_contract.behavior: Stores v into total and returns *this. Same chaining evidence as set_progress; it is the second link in `.set_progress(60).set_total(200)`.

Returns a percentage string, i.e. it DELEGATES to Format::percentage(progress as f32 / total as f32, 1). It returns std::string (not a stream-manipulator object): main does `__ostream_insert(cout, str_data, len)` on the result and then destroys it with ~basic_string. Delegation is proven by the inlined code at 0x40245a-0x40249d being an exact clone of Format::percentage's body (precision=1, std::fixed, _M_insert<double>, then "%"), with the value constant-folded to the double at .rodata 0x404060 = 0x403E000020000000 = 30.0000019073486328125. That constant equals (f32)(0.3f32 * 100.0f32), which pins down BOTH that the arithmetic is f32 (a double pipeline would have folded to exactly 30.0 = 0x403E000000000000) AND the operation order: divide first, then multiply by 100 ((60/200)*100 -> 0x41f00001; (60*100)/200 -> 0x41f00000, only the former matches).

api_contract.cpp_signature: class ProgressTracker { int progress_ = 0; int total_ = 100; std::vector<std::string> stages_; };
api_contract.rust_signature: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Default)] pub struct ProgressTracker { progress: i32, total: i32, stages: Vec<String> }
api_contract.behavior: Layout and defaults are DIRECTLY OBSERVED, not guessed: at 0x40259d main does `mov 0x404068,%rax; mov %rax,0x40(%rsp)`, and .rodata:0x404068 holds the 8 bytes 00 00 00 00 64 00 00 00 = {i32 0, i32 100}. So progress is at +0 with default 0 and total is at +4 with default 100. Then `movups %xmm0,0x48(%rsp)` + `movq $0x0,0x58(%rsp)` zero a 24-byte std::vector<std::string> at offset +8 (destroyed at 0x402abb via ~vector). Note Default cannot be derived if total defaults to 100 - write `impl Default` by hand returning { progress: 0, total: 100, stages: Vec::new() }.

api_contract.rust_signature: pub fn add_stage(&mut self, name: &str) -> &mut Self
api_contract.behavior: Pushes name onto the stages vector and returns *this so calls chain (call site chains three: .add_stage("Downloading").add_stage("Processing").add_stage("Saving")). The parameter type is const std::string& (NOT const char*): for each literal the binary first constructs a temporary via `basic_string(char const*, allocator)` from .rodata (0x404020 "Downloading", 0x40402c "Processing", 0x404037 "Saving") and then calls `vector<string>::push_back(std::string const&)`; a const char* parameter would need no temporary. In Rust take &str and do stages.push(name.to_string()). Stages are stored but NEVER read - they contribute zero bytes to stdout.

api_contract.cpp_signature: void set_progress(int v)   // return type unobservable
api_contract.rust_signature: pub fn set_progress(&mut self, v: i32)
api_contract.behavior: Stores v into progress. Called as a standalone statement `tracker.set_progress(1);` - never chained - so unlike add_stage there is no evidence it returns a reference. GCC folded set_progress(1)+set_total(3) into ONE 8-byte store: `mov 0x404070,%rax; mov %rax,0x40(%rsp)` where .rodata:0x404070 = 01 00 00 00 03 00 00 00 = {i32 1, i32 3}. Returning () is the honest minimal choice; returning &mut Self would also satisfy the call site.

api_contract.cpp_signature: void set_total(int v)   // return type unobservable
api_contract.rust_signature: pub fn set_total(&mut self, v: i32)
api_contract.behavior: Stores v into total. Same evidence as set_progress (the two setters share the single folded {1,3} store). Both setters run BEFORE any printing, so get_progress() sees progress=1, total=3.

Returns format!("{}/{}", progress, total) - a std::string, NOT a numeric type and NOT a tuple. Inlined at 0x402711-0x40273d as: `mov $0x1,%esi; call std::ostream::operator<<(int)`, then `__ostream_insert(os, 0x40403e, 1)` where .rodata:0x40403e = "/" (a 1-char literal), then `mov $0x3,%esi; call std::ostream::operator<<(int)`, then oss.str(). Integer insertion via operator<<(int) means plain decimal, no padding, no thousands separators (default C locale), and a leading '-' for negatives - exactly Rust's Display for i32.

Returns Format::percentage(progress as f32 / total as f32, 1). Delegation and the exact float pipeline are visible in the inlined code at 0x4028f5-0x402954: `cvtsi2ssl 0x40(%rsp),%xmm0` (i32 progress -> f32), `cvtsi2ssl 0x44(%rsp),%xmm1` (i32 total -> f32), `divss %xmm1,%xmm0` (f32 divide), `mulss 0x404040` (x 100.0f in f32), `cvtss2sd`, precision=1 (`movq $0x1,0x8(%rdx)`), std::fixed, _M_insert<double>, `__ostream_insert("%",1)`. Crucially there is NO branch testing total for zero, so there is no divide-by-zero guard: total=0 yields inf/nan and prints "inf%"/"-nan%" in C++. Unreachable from these call sites.

api_contract.cpp_signature: std::vector<std::string> stages_;  // private, never read in this TU
api_contract.rust_signature: pub fn stages(&self) -> &[String]   // optional, recommended over #[allow(dead_code)]
api_contract.behavior: The stages vector is written (3 push_backs) and destroyed, never read - it produces no output. Keep the field private. Because nothing reads it, rustc will emit a `field is never read` warning; resolve that with ONE minimal honest accessor `pub fn stages(&self) -> &[String] { &self.stages }` (and optionally `pub fn stage_count(&self) -> usize`), or with #[allow(dead_code)] on the field. Do NOT invent current_stage/advance/next_stage/render - none of that is observable in the binary or the call sites.

result.format_rules:
EXACT OUTPUT: 5 lines, 29 bytes total, each terminated by a single \n, no trailing blank line, exit code 0:
  "30.0%\n" (6) + "1/3\n" (4) + "33.3%\n" (6) + "33.0%\n" (6) + "66.00%\n" (7) = 29 bytes.

THE ONE MASTER RULE (percentage rendering), reverse-engineered from the disassembly of indicators::Format::percentage at 0x402f00:
  C++:  std::ostringstream oss; oss << std::fixed << std::setprecision(precision) << (value * 100.0f) << "%"; return oss.str();
  Rust: format!("{:.*}%", precision, (value * 100.0f32) as f64)
Three details matter and all three are pinned by machine code, not guesswork:
  (a) `mulss` (not mulsd) with the f32 constant 100.0f at .rodata:0x404040 -> the multiply happens in f32 and the product is ROUNDED BACK TO f32 before printing.
  (b) `cvtss2sd` then _M_insert<double> -> the f32 product is promoted to double for formatting. f32->f64 promotion is exact, so `as f64` is semantically a no-op for the digit string (verified: {:.10} on the f32 and on the promoted f64 both give "33.3333358765", matching C printf "%.10f"). Keep the `as f64` anyway to mirror the C++ path.
  (c) `and $0xfffffefb; or $0x4` on ios_base::_M_flags = clear floatfield(0x104), set _S_fixed(0x4) = `std::fixed`; `movslq %esi,%r14` -> _M_precision. Rust's `{:.N}` on a float is the exact equivalent of std::fixed+setprecision(N): both print exactly N fractional digits with no exponent. Rounding agrees because both glibc printf and Rust round the EXACT binary value half-to-even (verified with a C program: 12.5 -> "12" and 6.25 -> "6.2" in both). N=0 omits the decimal point in both.
The '%' is a literal 1-char suffix (`__ostream_insert(os, 0x404004 /* "%" */, 1)`), inside the returned string - not added by the caller.

DERIVED VALUE RULE for build()/get_percentage(): value = progress as f32 / total as f32, i.e. DIVIDE FIRST, THEN multiply by 100.0f32. get_percentage's inlined `cvtsi2ssl; cvtsi2ssl; divss; mulss` shows this literally, and build()'s folded constant proves it independently: .rodata:0x404060 = 0x403E000020000000 = 30.0000019073486328125 = (f32)(0.3f32*100.0f32); the other order (60*100)/200 would have folded to exactly 30.0 = 0x403E000000000000. Both orders happen to print "30.0", but only div-then-mul reproduces the binary's arithmetic, and it is what a general-purpose port must use.

LINE-BY-LINE, with the exact Rust expression for each:

Line 1 -> "30.0%"   from `builder.build()` with progress=60, total=200.
  Rust: println!("{}", builder.build());
  where build() == Format::percentage(self.progress as f32 / self.total as f32)
  Evaluation: 60f32/200f32 = 0.3f32 (bits 0x3e99999a); 0.3f32*100.0f32 = 30.000002f32 (bits 0x41f00001); as f64 = 30.0000019073486328125 (bits 0x403e000020000000, byte-identical to the constant embedded in the reference binary); {:.1} -> "30.0"; + '%' -> "30.0%". Note it is NOT exactly 30.0 - the f32 error is invisible only because it is far below the 1-decimal rounding threshold.

Line 2 -> "1/3"     from `tracker.get_progress()` with progress=1, total=3 (both setters ran before the print).
  Rust: println!("{}", tracker.get_progress());
  where get_progress() == format!("{}/{}", self.progress, self.total)
  Plain i32 Display on both sides of a literal '/'. No padding, no width, no locale grouping, no percent sign, no floats involved.

Line 3 -> "33.3%"   from `tracker.get_percentage()` with progress=1, total=3.
  Rust: println!("{}", tracker.get_percentage());
  where get_percentage() == Format::percentage(self.progress as f32 / self.total as f32)
  Evaluation: 1f32/3f32 = 0.33333334f32 (bits 0x3eaaaaab); *100.0f32 = 33.333336f32; as f64 = 33.33333587646484375; {:.1} -> "33.3"; + '%' -> "33.3%".

Line 4 -> "33.0%"   from `Format::percentage(0.33f)` using the DEFAULT precision of 1.
  Rust: println!("{}", Format::percentage(0.33f32));   // -> percentage_with_precision(0.33f32, 1)
  Evaluation: the literal is an f32 (binary passes .rodata:0x404044 = c3 f5 a8 3e = 0x3ea8f5c3 = 0.33f32 = 0.32999999821186065673828125, and the callee reads it from xmm0 as 4 bytes); *100.0f32 rounds to exactly 33.0f32; {:.1} -> "33.0"; + '%' -> "33.0%". Do NOT write 0.33f64 - use `0.33f32` so the value is the f32 the C++ compiler emitted.

Line 5 -> "66.00%"  from `Format::percentage(0.66f, 2)` with EXPLICIT precision 2.
  Rust: println!("{}", Format::percentage_with_precision(0.66f32, 2));
  Evaluation: literal from .rodata:0x404048 = c3 f5 28 3f = 0x3f28f5c3 = 0.66f32 = 0.660000026226043701171875; *100.0f32 rounds to exactly 66.0f32; {:.2} -> "66.00"; + '%' -> "66.00%". This line is the proof that precision is a real parameter and that trailing zeros are PRESERVED (fixed notation, not shortest-representation) - a naive `{}` or a trim-trailing-zeros helper would print "66%" and fail.

I/O MECHANICS: `std::cout << s << std::endl` five times. std::endl writes '\n' and flushes; flushing changes no bytes, so five `println!` calls are byte-equivalent. Use println! (or one write! of the whole 29-byte payload). Do not print a 6th newline. Return exit code 0 (fall off main / no explicit process::exit needed).

CLI: the C++ binary declares main(argc, argv) but never touches either (no argv reads in the disassembly of main) and its output is unchanged by `foo bar 42` (verified). test5.rs must call std::env::args() at least once to satisfy the requirement, discard the result, and never panic or error: e.g. `let _args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().collect();` then ignore it. Do not index into args (that panics on absent args) and do not validate/reject extras.

VERIFIED END TO END: a 5-line Rust probe using exactly the expressions above (/tmp/probe/q.rs, built with rustc 1.75.0) cmp's clean (29 bytes) against /workspace/dataset/test5_executable, including with extra argv. A reconstructed C++ header (/tmp/cxx/include/indicators.hpp) implementing this contract, compiled with g++-12 -O2 -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0 against the verbatim /workspace/dataset/test5.cpp, also produces byte-identical output and the same divss/mulss/cvtss2sd codegen shape.
open_questions: ProgressBuilder's default field values are genuinely unobservable: both are overwritten by set_progress(60)/set_total(200) and GCC constant-folded the entire object away, so no builder is ever materialized on main's stack. I recommend {progress: 0, total: 100} by symmetry with ProgressTracker (whose {0, 100} defaults ARE visible as the 8 bytes at .rodata:0x404068). This choice cannot affect any of the 5 output lines.

ProgressTracker::set_progress / set_total return types are unobservable: both call sites are standalone statements (`tracker.set_progress(1);`), never chained, and GCC folded the pair into a single 8-byte store of {1,3}. I chose `()` (C++ void) as the honest minimum. Returning `&mut Self` for symmetry with add_stage would also satisfy the call sites - pick one and be consistent.

Division-by-zero behavior diverges between C++ and Rust and is unreachable from these call sites, so it is a design choice, not a constraint. There is provably no guard in the C++ (no test/branch on total before divss), so total=0 gives inf/nan; C++ then prints "inf%" / "-nan%" while Rust prints "inf%" / "NaN%" (capitalization and nan sign differ). If you want bit-faithful behavior beyond the observed inputs, keep the unguarded f32 divide and document the divergence; do not add an early-return guard, which would silently change semantics.

The precision parameter is `int` in C++ (confirmed by `movslq %esi,%r14` sign-extending a 32-bit value into _M_precision). Rust's `{:.N}` needs a usize, so negative precisions are unrepresentable. In C++ a negative setprecision reaches snprintf's "%.*f" and yields the default 6 digits. Only 1 and 2 are ever used, so I recommend `precision: usize`; use `i32` only if you also want to emulate the negative case.

Whether the real header spells the helper as a static member of a `Format` class or as a free function in the namespace is not fully determined - the mangled name `indicators::Format::percentage(float, int)` proves a class/struct-scoped static (a free function would mangle as `indicators::percentage`), but whether `Format` is `class` or `struct` and whether it has other unused static members that were never instantiated is unknowable. The single-associated-function unit struct is the faithful minimum.

Whether build()/get_percentage() textually call Format::percentage or duplicate its body is not strictly provable, since both were inlined. The inlined instruction sequences are exact clones of Format::percentage's body (same std::fixed flag manipulation, same 100.0f constant at 0x404040, same "%" at 0x404004, same precision literal 1), so delegation is by far the best explanation and is also the DRY choice. Delegating is behaviorally identical either way, so nothing observable rides on this.

Rust module layout is not dictated by the contract, only by the deliverable's "organized into MODULES" plus dual-build requirement. A layout that satisfies both `rustc test5.rs` and `cargo build --release`: /output/test5.rs declares `#[path = "src/indicators/mod.rs"] mod indicators;` (the #[path] resolves relative to test5.rs's own directory, so bare rustc works), with src/indicators/mod.rs re-exporting src/indicators/{format,builder,tracker}.rs, and Cargo.toml carrying `[[bin]] name = "test5", path = "test5.rs"`. Confirm the parent agent wants this exact shape before committing to it.

edge_cases: FRAMING: every item below is UNEXERCISED by the 29-byte ground truth. Nothing in the reference output constrains any of it, so every choice here is a deliberate, unverifiable bet about untested behavior. Recommend documenting that in a code comment rather than silently picking.

NaN SPELLING (the one confirmed formatting divergence): C++/glibc prints 'nan'/'-nan' (sign-bit aware); Rust prints 'NaN' always, ignoring the sign bit. Worse, on x86-64 0.0f/0.0f yields a NEGATIVE quiet NaN, so C++ actually prints '-nan', not 'nan' -- the brief's expected 'nan' is itself off. Three-way mismatch: C++ '-nan' vs C++ 'nan' vs Rust 'NaN'. Reachable via total=0 AND progress=0. Strict parity would need an explicit shim: match on is_nan() then sign_bit to emit 'nan'/'-nan', since no Rust format flag produces lowercase 'nan'.

INFINITY: NO divergence, contrary to the brief's framing. Both print exactly 'inf' and '-inf' (verified). So a total=0, progress>0 case already agrees byte-for-byte with C++ WITHOUT any guard. This is a positive argument for not guarding: an IEEE-faithful Rust port matches C++ on the inf cases and only misses on the rarer 0/0 NaN case.

INTEGER DIVISION PANIC (strongest real reason to guard, unrelated to formatting): Rust float division by zero never panics, but `progress * 100 / total` in INTEGER types panics with 'attempt to divide by zero' in both debug and release. C++ integer div-by-zero is UB and typically SIGFPE. If any part of the port (e.g. a shortcut for line 1) uses integer arithmetic, total==0 must be guarded or the 'must not panic on any args' requirement is violated. Recommendation: keep all percentage math in floating point so IEEE semantics apply and no guard is needed for panic-safety.

NEGATIVE / SIGNED TOTALS: formatting is safe -- 1/-3*100 prints '-33.3' identically in both, and -0.0 prints '-0.0' identically. The risk is in the TYPE, not the formatting: line 2 is format!("{}/{}", progress, total), so if the Rust port uses u64/usize while the C++ used `int`, total=-3 is unrepresentable and any `-1i64 as u64` conversion silently yields 18446744073709551615. If the C++ used size_t, C++ wraps the same way; if it used int, C++ prints '-3'. Unknowable black-box. Recommend i64/i32 for progress/total so the ratio line can render negatives the way an int-based C++ API would, and do not add clamping.

HUGE FINITE VALUES: safe, no divergence. Both languages emit the FULL exact decimal expansion at fixed precision -- 1e30 at p=1 gives '1000000000000000019884624838656.0' in both (31 integer digits). A huge total produces an identically long line in both: no truncation, no scientific-notation fallback. f32::MAX*100 overflows to 'inf' in both.

PRECISION EXTREMES: setprecision(0) gives '33' (no decimal point) in C++ and '{:.0}' gives '33' in Rust -- match. Large precision (verified at p=6) also matches; both pad with exact expansion digits then zeros. API-shape (not value) divergence: C++ setprecision takes int so a negative precision is expressible, whereas Rust's {:.*} takes usize and cannot be negative.

GUARDING RECOMMENDATION (explicit): do NOT add a value-changing guard such as `if total <= 0 { return "0.0%" }`. It would break the inf cases that currently match C++ exactly, it is unverifiable against the reference, and it trades a confirmed match for an invented behavior. Instead: (a) keep percentage math in f32/f64 so division by zero cannot panic; (b) if any integer division is used anywhere, guard only that to avoid the panic; (c) leave a comment stating the 29-byte contract never exercises total<=0, so IEEE semantics were chosen deliberately over a guard. If a future spec demands C++ parity on 0/0, add the lowercase nan/-nan shim rather than a guard.
result.equivalence_verdict:
PROVEN EQUIVALENT for all four float-formatted lines (1, 3, 4, 5); line 2 is pure integer formatting with zero FP risk. C++ `std::fixed << std::setprecision(N)` (glibc/libstdc++) and Rust `{:.N$}` agree on every one of these values, and the agreement is structural, not luck.

WHY THEY AGREE: both implementations perform *exact* arbitrary-precision binary->decimal conversion of the full value, then round the exact decimal expansion at digit N using round-half-to-even. Neither does a shortest-roundtrip repr followed by a second rounding (which is where most cross-language formatters diverge). Decisive evidence: `{:.1}` and `%.1f` on 1e30 BOTH print "1000000000000000019884624838656.0" -- the complete 31-digit exact expansion of the double, not "1000000000000000000000000000000.0". A shortest-repr-then-pad implementation cannot produce that string.

Ties-to-even confirmed empirically in BOTH, identically: 0.25@p1 -> "0.2", 0.75@p1 -> "0.8", 2.5@p0 -> "2", 3.5@p0 -> "4", 66.125@p2 -> "66.12", 66.375@p2 -> "66.38".

IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO THE TASK PREMISE: the brief states "0.33f32 has exact value 0.3299999883651733398437500". That is wrong, and the true value moves in the OPPOSITE direction. 0.33f32 = 0.3300000131130218505859375 exactly (bits 0x3ea8f5c3) -- it rounds UP, not down. The brief's claimed constant is not even a representable f32 (it round-trips to 0.3299999833106994628906250 = bits 0x3ea8f5c2 = nextbelow(0.33f)). The verdict is unaffected: I formatted both spellings explicitly and both give "33.0" at precision 1 in both languages. The brief's Q3 premise is also wrong -- see recommended_arithmetic.

NO TIE BOUNDARIES. Note the correct argument is NOT "binary floats can never be decimal ties" -- they can. 0.25 is an exact tie at p=1; 66.125 is an exact tie at p=2. A tie at precision p requires value = m/10^(p+1) with 5^(p+1) | m, which dyadic rationals can satisfy. The correct argument is that our four values are FAR from ties. Measured distance to the nearest rounding-decision boundary, in f32 ULPs:
  L1 30.0000019073486328 @p1 -> 0.0499980927 away = 26213.4 ULP
  L3 33.3333358764648438 @p1 -> 0.0166641235 away =  4368.4 ULP
  L4 33.0 (exact)        @p1 -> 0.0500000000 away = 13107.2 ULP
  L5 66.0 (exact)        @p2 -> 0.0050000000 away =   655.4 ULP  <- tightest
The tightest margin is 655 ULPs of f32.

Beyond the 5 required values I ran a 300,871-case randomized differential test (random f32 bit patterns at precisions 0-3, plus 40,000 structured exact-dyadic-tie cases at .125/.25/.375/.5/.625/.75/.875): byte-identical between g++ and rustc, zero mismatches.

END-TO-END PROOF: a modular Rust program built three different ways (pure-f32 multiply, widen-then-f64 multiply, all-f64 internal) produced byte-identical 29-byte output matching /workspace/dataset/test5_executable under `cmp`, both with no argv and with extra argv "foo bar 42", exit 0.

The ONLY divergence found anywhere is the NaN spelling, which the 29-byte contract never exercises (see edge_cases).

result.recommended_arithmetic:
RECOMMENDATION: f32 multiply, then widen for formatting.
    pub fn percentage(v: f32, prec: usize) -> String {
        format!("{:.*}%", prec, (v * 100.0f32) as f64)
    }
and compute internal fractions in f32: `progress as f32 / total as f32`.

The `as f64` widen is cosmetic/optional -- proof (E) shows 31,457,280 comparisons in which
f32-direct and widened formatting never differ, because f32->f64 is an exact conversion and both
formatters expand exactly. Keep it only because it mirrors what C++ `ostream << float` does
(promotes to double), so the Rust source reads as a faithful transliteration.

CAN THE CHOICE CHANGE ANY OF THE 5 OUTPUT LINES? No -- proven three independent ways:
 1. Directly: all 18 FMT cases in evidence (C) cover both paths for every affected line and yield
    identical strings; the C++/Rust diff was byte-identical.
 2. End-to-end: proof (F) built the same modular program three ways (pure-f32, widen-then-f64,
    all-f64) and all three emitted the identical 29 bytes under `cmp` against the real binary.
 3. By margin analysis: the paths differ by at most one f32 ULP of the product (<=7.63e-06 near 66,
    <=3.81e-06 near 33, <=1.91e-06 near 30). The tightest rounding-decision margin among the 5
    lines is 0.005 absolute (line 5, "66.00" at p=2) = 655 f32 ULPs. The perturbation is ~3 orders
    of magnitude smaller than the margin, so no reachable arithmetic path can move a printed digit.
    Lines 1/3/4 have margins of 26213 / 4368 / 13107 ULPs respectively.

WHY PREFER f32 ANYWAY, GIVEN ALL PATHS PASS? Because the goal is byte-fidelity to an unseen
reference, not numerical accuracy. The C++ signature is Format::percentage(float, int) and the call
sites pass 0.33f / 0.66f, so idiomatic library code is `value * 100` or `value * 100.0f` -- an f32
multiply. If any un-shown input is ever exercised, an f32 Rust port matches the C++ bit-for-bit,
whereas an f64 port is *more accurate than the reference*, which in a byte-exact port is a
divergence risk rather than a benefit. Concretely, the two paths already disagree in the 7th
significant digit on line 1 (30.000001907348633 vs 30.000001192092896) and line 3
(33.333335876464844 vs 33.333334326744079) -- invisible at precision 1, but it would surface at
precision >= 6: Format::percentage(0.33f, 6) yields "33.000000%" on the f32 path and "33.000001%"
on the f64 path. Choosing f32 keeps that latent difference aligned with the most likely C++ source.

LINE-SPECIFIC NOTES:
 * Line 1 (ProgressBuilder{60,200}) could equally be integer arithmetic in the C++ original
   (60*100/200 = 30 -> "30.0"). That also produces "30.0", so it is unobservable here -- but see
   the integer-division panic risk in edge_cases before choosing an integer path.
 * Line 2 ("1/3") should be plain integer formatting, format!("{}/{}", progress, total). No
   floating point involved, so it carries zero formatting-equivalence risk.
 * Default precision for Format::percentage must be 1 (line 4 uses the default and prints "33.0");
   Rust has no default arguments, so expose percentage(v) delegating to percentage_prec(v, 1).

pitfalls: VALIDATED BOTH BUILD PATHS (clean, from scratch, minimal Cargo.toml above). (a) `cd /tmp/pkgcheck && rustc test5.rs` -> exit=0, ZERO output (no warnings), produced ./test5 (13285408 bytes); running it printed the 3 stub lines. (b) `cd /tmp/pkgcheck && cargo build --release` -> '   Compiling test5 v0.1.0 (/tmp/pkgcheck)' / '    Finished release [optimized] target(s) in 0.49s', exit=0, produced target/release/test5 (13264128 bytes). `diff <(./test5) <(./target/release/test5)` -> IDENTICAL. Also passes the stricter `rustc -D warnings test5.rs` (exit=0) and `RUSTFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo build --release` (exit=0).

#[path = "src/indicators/mod.rs"] mod indicators; RESOLVES FOR BOTH rustc and cargo. `cargo metadata --no-deps` confirms exactly one target: kind ["bin"], name "test5", src_path "/tmp/pkgcheck/test5.rs", edition "2021" — no lib target. Because cargo sets the bin path to test5.rs at the package root, #[path] is relative to /output in both cases.

NESTED SUBMODULES NEED NO FURTHER #[path]. Validated 3 levels deep: src/indicators/mod.rs declares plain `pub mod format;` and `pub mod progress;`, and src/indicators/progress/mod.rs declares plain `pub mod builder;` -> resolves to src/indicators/progress/builder.rs. Only the ONE #[path] on the root `mod indicators;` is needed; everything below resolves normally relative to its own directory.

BIGGEST TRAP — BARE `rustc test5.rs` DEFAULTS TO EDITION 2015, cargo uses 2021. The code must compile warning-free under BOTH. Verified OK in both editions on rustc 1.75: `crate::indicators::format` paths, `super::format as superfmt`, `use std::fmt::Write`, and `use indicators::progress::ProgressBuilder;` in test5.rs (works in 2021 too via uniform paths, since `mod indicators;` is in scope at the crate root). Do NOT pass --edition; requirement (a) is literally `rustc test5.rs`.

EDITION-DIVERGENT WARNING that breaks warning-freedom on path (a) only: calling `.into_iter()` on an ARRAY. `let arr = ["Downloading","Processing","Saving"]; arr.into_iter()` compiles under both editions but under 2015 emits: 'warning: this method call resolves to `<&[T; N] as IntoIterator>::into_iter` (due to backwards compatibility), but will resolve to <[T; N] as IntoIterator>::into_iter in Rust 2021 ... = warning: this changes meaning in Rust 2021 ... = note: `#[warn(array_into_iter)]` on by default'. Cargo/2021 is silent. FIX: use `.iter()`, or `IntoIterator::into_iter(arr)`, or build the stage list with `vec![...]` / repeated `add_stage` calls instead of an array literal. Same class of hazard: avoid `try`/`async`/`await` as identifiers (reserved in 2018+) and `panic!(non_str_expr)`.

DEAD_CODE: in a BIN crate `pub` does NOT exempt items. Real warning hit: 'warning: function `never_called_public_api` is never used --> src/indicators/format.rs:2:8 ... = note: `#[warn(dead_code)]` on by default' — emitted IDENTICALLY by rustc and by cargo ('warning: `test5` (bin "test5") generated 1 warning'). FIX that I validated: put crate-level inner attribute `#![allow(dead_code)]` at the very TOP of test5.rs (above the #[path] attribute). One crate-root allow silences the whole #[path]-included module tree. Add a comment explaining why: the port mirrors the full C++ public API surface (e.g. ProgressBuilder::set_progress/set_total, add_stage, Format::percentage with both arities) but main() only exercises part of it, and there is no lib target to make those items externally reachable.

UNUSED-ARG WARNING: `let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().collect();` left unused emits 'warning: unused variable: `args` ... help: if this is intentional, prefix it with an underscore: `_args`'. Bind as `_args` (validated warning-free) or actually consume it. Reference binary ignores argv entirely — verified `./test5_executable foo bar 42` still emits the same 29 bytes, exit 0 — so parse-and-ignore is correct; never index argv or unwrap/parse it (would panic on extra args).

DO NOT ADD A [lib] TARGET over the same sources — validated failure. With `[lib] name="indicators" path="src/indicators/mod.rs"` alongside the [[bin]], cargo compiles mod.rs a SECOND time as its own crate root, where `crate::` now means the indicators module itself: 'error[E0432]: unresolved import `crate::indicators` --> src/indicators/progress/builder.rs:1:12 | use crate::indicators::format; | ^^^^^^^^^^ could not find `indicators` in the crate root' / 'error: could not compile `test5` (lib) due to previous error', exit=101. Bare rustc still succeeded in that layout, so this breaks ONLY path (b) — easy to miss if you test rustc first.

DO NOT omit [[bin]] hoping autodiscovery works — there is no src/main.rs, so: 'error: failed to parse manifest at `/tmp/pkgbad1/Cargo.toml` / Caused by: no targets specified in the manifest / either src/lib.rs, src/main.rs, a [lib] section, or [[bin]] section must be present', exit=101. Conversely, cargo does NOT warn about test5.rs living at the package root, does NOT warn about the missing src/main.rs, and does NOT warn about `edition = "2021"` with no lib target. No `autobins = false` needed: files under src/indicators/ are never autodiscovered (only src/lib.rs, src/main.rs, src/bin/*.rs, examples/, tests/, benches/ are).

target/ ARTIFACTS AND THE ROOT BINARY CAUSE NO PROBLEM, IN EITHER ORDER. Validated all four interleavings: rustc-then-cargo, cargo-then-rustc, cargo twice, and cargo with both ./test5 and target/ already present — all exit=0. rustc writes ./test5 in the package root and cargo writes target/release/test5; they never collide because the names live in different directories. cargo also silently generates Cargo.lock (harmless). A .gitignore is irrelevant — cargo never mentions it; `target/` in one is fine but optional.

#[path] IS RESOLVED RELATIVE TO THE CONTAINING FILE'S DIRECTORY, NOT THE CWD — verified by `cd /tmp/elsewhere && rustc /tmp/pkgcheck/test5.rs`, which compiled fine (exit=0) but dropped the binary at /tmp/elsewhere/test5. So the deliverable must be built as `cd /output && rustc test5.rs` to land the executable at /output/test5 as required.

OUTPUT BYTE-EXACTNESS IS ACHIEVABLE WITH PLAIN f32 + `format!` — verified independently: `fn pct(v: f32, prec: usize) -> String { format!("{:.*}%", prec, v * 100.0) }` with pct(60f32/200f32,1), "1/3" via format!("{}/{}"), pct(1f32/3f32,1), pct(0.33f32,1), pct(0.66f32,2) produced xxd '3330 2e30 250a 312f 330a 3333 2e33 250a 3333 2e30 250a 3636 2e30 3025 0a' = exactly the target 29 bytes "30.0%
1/3
33.3%
33.0%
66.00%
". Use f32 (NOT f64) to match the C++ float semantics, and `{:.*}` for the runtime precision argument. No value here sits on a rounding half-way boundary, so Rust's round-half-to-even formatting matches. Emit with println! (single 
 each, no trailing blank line); stdout is line-buffered to a pipe but flushed at exit, so no manual flush needed.

Recommended module split satisfying 'modules, not one file': src/indicators/mod.rs (declares `pub mod format; pub mod progress;` and optionally re-exports), src/indicators/format.rs (Format::percentage with default precision 1 — Rust has no default args, so provide `percentage(v)` delegating to `percentage_with_precision(v, 1)`, or an inherent-impl pair on a `Format` unit struct), src/indicators/progress/mod.rs (`pub mod builder; pub mod tracker;`), src/indicators/progress/builder.rs (ProgressBuilder with chainable `set_progress`/`set_total` returning `&mut Self` to mirror the C++ fluent chaining, plus `build()`), src/indicators/progress/tracker.rs (ProgressTracker with `add_stage` returning `&mut Self`, `set_progress`, `set_total`, `get_progress()` -> "1/3", `get_percentage()` -> "33.3%"). Note builder.build() returns the formatted percentage String ("30.0%"), not a bar.

files.purpose: Package manifest. Single [[bin]] target name="test5", path="test5.rs", edition 2021. No [lib], no autodiscovered targets.

Entry point at the package root. One `#[path = "src/indicators/mod.rs"] mod indicators;`, `use indicators::{Format, ProgressBuilder, ProgressTracker};`, reads and ignores std::env::args() as `_args`, then five println! calls reproducing the 29 bytes. No library logic.

Module hub: `pub mod format/progress_builder/progress_tracker;`, `pub use self::...` re-exports (self:: is mandatory for edition-2015 bare rustc), and `pub(crate) fn ratio(progress: i32, total: i32) -> f32` encoding the divide-first, float-only, unguarded fraction.

`pub const DEFAULT_PRECISION: usize = 1;`, unit struct `Format`, `Format::percentage(f32) -> String` delegating to `Format::percentage_with_precision(f32, usize) -> String` which returns format!("{scaled:.precision$}%") over f64::from(value * 100.0f32).

`ProgressBuilder { progress: i32, total: i32 }` (Debug+Clone+Copy), `new()` = {0,100}, hand-written Default, chainable `set_progress`/`set_total` returning `&mut Self`, `build(&self) -> String` delegating to Format::percentage(ratio(..)).

`ProgressTracker { progress: i32, total: i32, stages: Vec<String> }` (Debug+Clone), `new()` = {0,100,vec![]}, hand-written Default, chainable `add_stage(&str) -> &mut Self`, void `set_progress`/`set_total`, `stages()` accessor with the single item-scoped #[allow(dead_code)], `get_progress()` -> "{}/{}", `get_percentage()` -> Format::percentage(ratio(..)).

risks: EDITION-2015 IMPORT TRAP (highest risk; all three analysts missed the concrete failure). Bare `rustc test5.rs` compiles as edition 2015, where `use`/`pub use` paths inside a non-root module are crate-relative. Writing `pub use format::Format;` in src/indicators/mod.rs fails with error[E0432]: unresolved import `format` under rustc while compiling fine under cargo/2021 — it breaks build path (a) only, so it is invisible if you test cargo first. I hit and fixed this. Mitigation: `pub use self::format::Format;` in every mod.rs and `use super::{ratio, Format};` in every sibling file. Both forms are valid in 2015 and 2021.

Adding a [lib] target over src/indicators/mod.rs breaks build path (b) only (mod.rs becomes a second crate root, `crate::indicators` no longer resolves, E0432, exit 101) while bare rustc still succeeds. Never declare [lib]. Conversely, omitting [[bin]] is a hard manifest error since there is no src/main.rs.

Speculative getters are warnings. `progress()`, `total()`, `stage_count()` and friends trigger dead_code in a bin crate (pub does NOT exempt items there) and would break `-D warnings`. Keep exactly the API in the spec, with the single item-scoped #[allow(dead_code)] on ProgressTracker::stages. Note also that the `stages` field currently avoids a `never read` warning both via that accessor and via #[derive(Debug)]; do not drop both the accessor and the Debug derive.

Any integer arithmetic in the percentage path (e.g. shortcutting line 1 as 60*100/200) reintroduces a divide-by-zero PANIC on total==0, violating "must not panic on any args". Keep everything in f32 via ratio() and add no guard: unguarded IEEE division matches the C++ on inf/-inf exactly, and only the unreachable 0/0 case diverges (C++ `-nan` vs Rust `NaN`).

Formatting shortcuts that print the wrong bytes: `{}` / `{:?}` / any shortest-representation or trailing-zero-trimming helper renders line 5 as `66%` instead of `66.00%`. Only `std::fixed`-equivalent `{:.N$}` (or `{:.*}`) is acceptable. Likewise the `%` must be inside the returned String, not appended by the caller.

Wrong float literal suffixes: `0.33` / `0.33f64` instead of `0.33f32`, or doing the *100 in f64, changes latent behavior (Format::percentage(0.33, 6) yields "33.000000%" on the f32 path vs "33.000001%" on the f64 path). It does not change the 29 bytes, but it drifts from the C++ `float` reference.

rustc writes its output binary into the CWD, not next to the source: `cd /tmp && rustc /output/test5.rs` silently lands the binary in /tmp. The deliverable requires exactly `cd /output && rustc test5.rs` so /output/test5 is produced.

Analyst 1's exact-decimal constants for 0.33f32/0.66f32 are wrong (0.33f32 rounds UP to 0.3300000131130218505859375, and 0.33f32*100.0f32 is exactly 33.0f32). Do not copy those digits into comments; the bit patterns 0x3ea8f5c3 / 0x3f28f5c3 are correct.
Six newlines. `println!` five times is exactly right; an extra `println!()`, a `\n` inside a returned String, or writeln! after the last line makes 30 bytes.

Extra arg handling: never index std::env::args() (args().nth(1).unwrap() panics), never parse or reject extras. Collect into `_args` and ignore; a plain `args` binding is itself an unused-variable warning.
